items.title: Ergodic partial sums, time averages and the invariant L2 subspace
items.statement: For a measure-preserving system (X,A,μ,T), a scalar measurable representative f and n≥1, define S_n f=Σ_{k=0}^{n-1}f∘T^k and A_n f=n^{-1}S_n f. In complex L2 set M={f:f∘T=f μ-a.e.}. The companion proposition proves that these formulas descend to Lp classes.
items.strategy: Fix T^0=id and the representative convention before any theorem uses A_n. M is the fixed space of the Koopman isometry, not an assertion that invariant functions are constant.

items.title: Ergodic averages are measurable, representative independent and Lp contractions
items.statement: Let T preserve μ. For every 1≤p≤∞, composition U_T[f]=[f∘T] is a well-defined linear isometry of real or complex Lp(μ). Hence S_n and A_n are well-defined measurable classes and ||A_n f||_p≤||f||_p.
items.strategy: Inverse images of measurable and null sets give measurability and representative independence. Integral invariance applied to |f|^p gives equality for finite p; inverse images preserve essential bounds for p=∞. Finish with Minkowski.

items.title: Maximal ergodic theorem
items.statement: Let T preserve an arbitrary measure μ and let f be a real-valued measurable representative in calligraphic L1(μ), before quotienting by a.e. equality. With S_n f unnormalised, E={x:sup_{n≥1}S_n f(x)>0} satisfies ∫_E f dμ≥0. No finiteness of μ or invertibility of T is assumed.
items.strategy: For N put F_N=max(0,S_1f,…,S_Nf) and E_N={F_N>0}. Positivity gives F_N∘T+f≥F_N on E_N. Since F_N vanishes off E_N, nonnegativity and integral invariance yield ∫_{E_N}f≥∫F_N−∫F_N∘T=0. Now E_N↑E; apply monotone convergence separately to f^+1_{E_N} and f^-1_{E_N}. Strict positivity and unnormalised sums are essential.

items.title: Sigma-finite oscillation sets have finite measure
items.statement: Let μ be sigma-finite, T preserve μ, and f∈L1(μ) be real. For rationals β<α, E_{α,β}={liminf_n A_nf<β<α<limsup_n A_nf} is invariant modulo null sets and has finite measure.
items.strategy: The shift identity makes both limiting envelopes invariant a.e.; replace E by its strict invariant representative. If α>0 and C is a finite-measure subset, apply the maximal theorem to f−α1_C: every point of E enters {sup S_n(f−α1_C)>0}, whence αμ(C)≤||f||_1. Exhaust by finite-measure sets. If α≤0, apply this to −f with threshold −β>0.

items.title: Birkhoff pointwise ergodic theorem
items.statement: Let μ be sigma-finite, T preserve μ, and let f be a real- or complex-valued measurable representative in calligraphic L1(μ). Then A_nf converges μ-a.e. to an integrable function f*, and f*∘T=f* μ-a.e. The resulting a.e. class depends only on the a.e. class of f. No ergodicity, finite total measure, completeness or invertibility is assumed.
items.strategy: For real f, cover the failure set by rational oscillation sets. Each has finite measure; the maximal inequality on a strict invariant representative, first for f at α and then −f at −β, forces αμ(E)≤∫_E f≤βμ(E), hence nullity. The shift identity proves invariance. Fatou applied to |A_nf| bounds ||f*||_1 and excludes infinite limits. Apply the result to real and imaginary parts.

items.title: Finite-measure identification of the Birkhoff limit
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If μ(X)<∞ and I={E∈A:T^{-1}E=E} is the strict invariant sigma-algebra, then for every E∈I, ∫_E f* dμ=∫_E f dμ. Moreover f* has an I-measurable representative, unique up to μ-a.e. equality, with these identities.
items.strategy: For invariant E, 1_EA_nf=A_n(f1_E) a.e. Derive both integral inequalities directly from the maximal inequality on rational level slices of f*, without consuming the later L1-convergence lemma. Define ν(E)=∫_E f on I; Radon–Nikodym gives an I-measurable density h. Each rational strict level set of f*−h is invariant modulo null sets; replace it by the explicit strict invariant representative, apply the event-integral identities, and use nonnegative integral order to force it null. Thus f*=h a.e. Treat real and imaginary components separately.

items.title: Ergodic averages also converge in Lp on finite-measure spaces
items.statement: Let μ(X)<∞, T preserve μ and 1≤p<∞. If f∈Lp and f* is its Birkhoff limit, then f*∈Lp and ||A_nf−f*||_p→0. No L∞ convergence is claimed.
items.strategy: For p=1 split |f| at K. On {|A_nf|>M}, contractivity and Markov give the uniform tail bound K||f||_1/M+||(|f|−K)_+||_1, hence uniform integrability; a.e. convergence implies convergence in measure and Vitali gives L1. For p>1 truncate f to bounded f_m. DCT gives Lp convergence of A_nf_m; contractivity and Fatou bound both remaining terms by ||f−f_m||_p. Bounded Lp norms alone are not used as uniform integrability of pth powers.

items.title: Unique ergodicity is equivalent to uniform ergodic averages
items.statement: Assume countable choice. For a continuous self-map T of a nonempty compact metric space K, the following are equivalent: (i) T is uniquely ergodic with invariant probability μ; (ii) for every real f∈C(K), A_nf converges uniformly on K to a constant. The constant is ∫f dμ.
items.strategy: If uniform convergence fails, choose n_j↑∞ and x_j witnessing fixed error and form empirical probabilities. A compact-probability subsequential limit ν is invariant by the telescoping identity, contradicting uniqueness. Conversely an empirical limit supplies existence; uniform convergence and invariance give identical continuous test integrals for every invariant probability, and the preceding lemma gives uniqueness.

items.title: Irrational circle rotations are uniquely ergodic
items.statement: Assume countable choice. If α is irrational, R_α on the circle is uniquely ergodic and its unique invariant Borel probability is Lebesgue measure.
items.strategy: For each continuous f, generic Birkhoff gives an invariant a.e. limit and the published ergodicity of R_α makes it constant. Since f is bounded, dominated convergence and integral invariance identify that constant as ∫f dλ, without the full-Choice Radon–Nikodym corollary. Every nonempty open circle arc has positive Lebesgue measure by the interval-measure formula, so the conull typical set is dense. Rotation is an isometry, hence uniform continuity of f makes {A_nf} equicontinuous; compactness gives a finite net of typical points and upgrades convergence to uniform convergence. Apply the uniform-average characterization. No Fourier series or Weyl criterion is used.

items.title: Canonical base-b expansions and normality
items.statement: For b≥2 and x∈[0,1), define d_j^(b)(x)=⌊bD_b^{j-1}x⌋ for j≥1, choosing at b-adic rationals the terminating expansion, equivalently the expansion not eventually b−1. items.title: FALSE: Birkhoff applies to every measurable function
items.statement: False claim: Birkhoff's finite a.e. convergence conclusion holds for every measurable finite-valued observable, without integrability.
items.strategy: On the ergodic doubling map take f(0)=0 and f(x)=1/x for x>0. Its strict superlevel sets are intervals (or the whole/empty set), so Borel-to-Lebesgue inclusion gives measurability. On the disjoint intervals [1/(k+1),1/k), f≥k, so the simple-function integral formula and the interval-measure formula give ∫f≥Σ_{k≥1}1/(k+1)=+∞ by harmonic-series divergence. Thus f is not integrable. For f_m=min(f,m), boundedness on this probability space makes f_m integrable, and monotone convergence gives ∫f_m↑+∞. Birkhoff makes its limit invariant; ergodicity makes that limit constant, while dominated convergence plus integral invariance identifies the constant as ∫f_m. Since f≥f_m, a countable intersection gives liminf A_nf=+∞ a.e. The L1 hypothesis is essential.

items.title: Borel normality has an uncountable null exceptional set
items.statement: Assume countable choice. The set C of canonical binary expansions whose even-position digits are all zero is uncountable, Lebesgue null, and contains no base-two normal number.
items.strategy: Fixing the first n even digits gives a union of cylinders of total mass 2^{-n}; continuity from above gives λ(C)=0. Map each subset of the positive integers to the canonical binary expansion having its chosen odd-position digits equal to one and all other digits zero. Every such string has infinitely many forced zero digits, so it is never an ambiguous eventually-one expansion; canonical existence and uniqueness make this a bijection onto C. Cantor's theorem and the surjective-enumeration criterion show that the power set of the positive integers, hence C, is uncountable. Every member has no occurrence of 11, so normality fails.

items.title: Initial terms of the square-root-two rotation
items.statement: For α=√2, the fractional parts {nα} for n=0,…,5 are approximately 0, 0.4142, 0.8284, 0.2426, 0.6569 and 0.0711; Weyl's theorem says the full sequence is equidistributed.
items.strategy: Subtract the integer part from n√2 for each listed n, then invoke irrationality of √2 and the Weyl theorem. The finite list illustrates rather than proves equidistribution.

items.title: A rational rotation has a nonconstant orbit average
items.statement: For R_{1/2} on the circle and f=1_[0,1/4), A_nf converges pointwise to (1/2)1_([0,1/4)∪[1/2,3/4)), a nonconstant invariant function.
items.strategy: Each orbit alternates x and x+1/2. Average the two values; odd partial averages have an error at most 1/n. The answer has integral 1/4 but is not the constant 1/4.

items.title: Kac's reciprocal return frequency recovered from Birkhoff
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. In an ergodic probability system, if μ(E)>0 and τ_m(x) is the time of the mth visit to E, then τ_m(x)/m→1/μ(E) for almost every x. This is the orbit-frequency form of Kac's reciprocal law.
items.strategy: Apply Birkhoff to 1_E to obtain N_E(n,x)/n→μ(E). At n=τ_m(x), the visit count differs from m only by the fixed indexing convention, so m/τ_m→μ(E); positivity permits reciprocals. Compare this orbitwise conclusion with the published Kac integral formula for first returns.

items.title: The fair-coin strong law as a shift average
items.statement: Assume countable choice. For a binary sequence x, A_n(x↦x_0)=n^{-1}Σ_{k<n}x_k; hence the fair-coin shift theorem gives convergence to 1/2 almost surely.
items.strategy: Compute the kth shifted coordinate observable as x_k, identify the average with the head frequency, and apply the page's fair-coin frequency theorem.

items.title: The periodic binary number 0.1010… is not normal
items.statement: The canonical binary number x=0.101010…_2=2/3 is not normal in base two: the block 00 has frequency zero rather than 1/4.
items.strategy: Sum the geometric series Σ_{j≥0}2^{-(2j+1)}=2/3. Its canonical expansion is periodic and not eventually one, so the convention applies directly; inspect adjacent pairs.

items.title: A nonintegrable observable can have infinite ergodic averages
items.statement: Assume countable choice. For the doubling map on ([0,1),λ), let f(0)=0 and f(x)=1/x for x>0. Then f is finite and measurable but not integrable, and A_nf(x)→+∞ for λ-almost every x.
items.strategy: The strict superlevel sets of f are intervals (or the whole/empty set), so Borel-to-Lebesgue inclusion makes f measurable. On each disjoint interval [1/(k+1),1/k), f≥k; the simple-function integral and interval-measure formulas therefore give ∫f≥Σ_{k≥1}1/(k+1)=+∞ by harmonic-series divergence, so f is not integrable. For f_m=min(f,m), boundedness on this probability space makes f_m integrable and monotone convergence gives ∫f_m↑+∞. Birkhoff makes the limit of A_nf_m invariant; ergodicity makes it constant, and dominated convergence plus integral invariance identifies the constant as ∫f_m. Intersect these conull sets over m; since f≥f_m, liminf_n A_nf dominates every truncated integral and is infinite.

items.title: The L2 projection for a nonergodic half-rotation
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For R_{1/2} and f=1_[0,1/4), the invariant-space projection is P_Mf=(1/2)1_([0,1/4)∪[1/2,3/4)); both the pointwise and L2 ergodic averages converge to this nonconstant function.
items.strategy: Even Cesaro sums are exactly the average of f and f∘R_{1/2}; odd sums differ by one term divided by n. The result is invariant and the residual changes sign under the half-rotation, hence is orthogonal to every invariant L2 function, identifying the projection.
